pageTwo.name: Local Rules
pageTwo.headline: CUT IT AND IT GROWS BACK.
pageTwo.dek: An interactive essay on cellular automata: six simulations running live on your own graphics card, from Conway’s Game of Life to a 33-kilobyte network that grows a butterfly and repairs it.
story: Every simulation in this essay runs on one idea: each cell on the grid looks only at its immediate neighbours, applies a single rule, and knows nothing about the picture it belongs to. Nobody tells the grid what to draw. The structure that appears — gliders, spots, stripes, whole organisms — is what falls out of that rule, applied everywhere at once.

There are six of them, ordered by how alive they get: Conway’s Game of Life, the wider rule space around it, Larger than Life, Lenia, reaction–diffusion, and finally a neural cellular automaton. All six are computed on your own GPU through WebGPU compute shaders — nothing here is a recorded video. On an Apple M-series chip under Metal 3, Conway sustains 5.8 billion cell updates per second on a 2048×2048 grid. Lenia’s much larger neighbourhood is convolved with an FFT instead, which overtakes direct convolution past a radius of about nine and runs 2.4× faster at Lenia’s radius of thirteen.

The last one was never programmed. It is a network of 8,336 numbers — 33 kilobytes, smaller than a screenshot of its own output — trained offline in PyTorch until a single lit pixel reliably grows into a butterfly. Drag the cursor through it and it does not restore a saved copy, because it doesn’t have one. Each surviving cell renegotiates with its neighbours, and the wing closes over the wound.

Every figure quoted above was measured on real hardware rather than estimated, and where the project’s own tables have no measurement they print a dash instead of a guess — a policy this newspaper warmly recommends to its competitors. —
